newsitem.title: UK: Global warming may be making, not melting, ice.
newsitem.headline: Global warming may be making, not melting, ice.

text.p: Global warming may be melting away some of the delicate ice shelves around the Antarctic, but not all of them, a British expert reported on Wednesday.
Climate change was actually causing some ice shelves to grow thicker, Keith Nicholls, an oceanographer with the British Antarctic Survey, said in a letter to the science journal Nature.
The "worrying" results illustrate that global warming does not bring uniform changes and can have unexpected effects.

"It's slightly worrying in a way to see the climate system has these tricks up its sleeve," Nicholls said in a statement. "It goes against common sense and makes you wonder how many other tricks it's got to catch us out."
Nicholls said said the smaller, more northerly ice shelves in the Antarctic were indeed melting in the heat.
But to see what was happening in the thicker, more southerly ice shelves his group examined the Filcher-Ronne shelf in the southern Weddell Sea.
"The most likely threat to the larger, more southerly ice shelves derives from their intimate thermal contact with the underlying ocean," Nicholls wrote.
His team used a hot-water drill to bore through the floating ice shelf and stuck sensors to the bottom to measure ice build-up.

They found that ocean circulation was indeed changing, but not in the way they would have predicted. Instead of warmer water coming in and melting the ice from underneath, cooler water was circulating and making the ice even thicker.
This was making the ice shelf stronger and less likely to break off, float away and melt -- the fate of thinnner shelves, Nicholls said.
The findings are of more than academic interest. "There is little doubt that the large Antarctic ice shelves are significant in the world's climate system," Nicholls said.
